name: Battle of Mohács
info: The Ottoman army under Suleiman the Magnificent defeated the Hungarian army of King Louis II near Mohács in 1526; Louis died in flight, and Hungary was later divided between the Ottomans, the Habsburgs and an eastern kingdom.

facts.place: A wide, waterlogged plain near the village of Mohács in the Kingdom of Hungary, on the Danube
facts.sides: The Kingdom of Hungary under King Louis II, with some 25,000 to 30,000 men at Mohács; the Ottoman Empire under Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent and the grand vizier Pargalı Ibrahim Pasha, perhaps 50,000, though some contemporary and modern historians put the number at 100,000
facts.outcome: The Hungarian army was encircled and its lines collapsed within two hours; King Louis II drowned in flight. The Ottomans took Buda, then withdrew.

t: Estimates of the Ottoman army run from about 45,000 to 100,000, while the Hungarians numbered some 25,000 to 30,000; the figures differ from passage to passage and between historians.

The Hungarian charge drove back the Ottoman front line, but Ibrahim Pasha's centre fell back in a crescent and the Hungarians, caught in the open between wings, cannon and Janissary fire, were encircled.
King Louis II and more than 1,000 nobles died, and about 2,000 captured Hungarians were executed afterwards; the kingdom was later split in three, and Hungarians still say 'More was lost at Mohács'.
dyk: King Louis II drowned in the marshy ground by the Csele stream, weighed down by his armour, and his body was found weeks later buried in the mud.

sections.background:
After the death of Matthias Corvinus in 1490, the Hungarian magnates, who did not want another heavy-handed king, procured the accession of Vladislaus of Bohemia, known as King Dobře, 'all right', for accepting every petition laid before him. He gave most of the royal estates and revenues to the nobility, and the nobles of the parliament cut their tax burden by 70 to 80%. The Black Army of Matthias was dissolved, and border guards and castle garrisons went unpaid. In 1514 a peasant rebellion led by György Dózsa was crushed by the nobles under John Zápolya, and Hungarians were no longer a politically united people.

In 1521 the Ottomans took Nándorfehérvár, present-day Belgrade, the strongest Hungarian fortress on the Danube, and Szabács, which left most of southern Hungary indefensible. In 1523 the aristocrats pledged funds for an army of 60,000 and 100 cannons to retake it, but the army, recruited late and without food, disbanded under hunger and disease without making the attempt. King Louis II married Mary of Habsburg in 1522, an alliance the Ottomans saw as a threat. The Porte made at least one and possibly two offers of peace, which Louis refused for unclear reasons.

In 1525 Francis I of France, defeated at Pavia, asked Suleiman to make war on the Holy Roman Empire; the road ran across Hungary, and the request suited Suleiman's ambitions. Louis appealed to the European princes, but only Henry VIII offered aid, which arrived in 1527, and the Pope offered 50,000 gold pieces. Charles V and Ferdinand of Austria did nothing, as the Habsburg armies were in Italy.
sections.forces:
The Hungarians gathered in three units: John Zápolya's Transylvanian army guarding the passes, between 8,000 and 13,000 men; the main army under Louis, with Spanish, German, Czech and Serbian mercenaries; and a smaller force of around 5,000 under the Croatian count Christoph Frankopan. At Mohács they numbered some 25,000 to 30,000. The known division by arms lists 3,000 armoured knights from the noble banderiums, the king's bodyguard of 1,000 armoured knights, 4,500 light cavalry, 6,700 infantry, mainly Hungarian, 5,300 papal infantry, mainly German Landsknechte, and 1,500 Polish infantry, with an unknown number of artillerymen. They had 85 cannons.

The Ottomans had the largest field artillery of the era, some 300 cannons. Their army at Mohács numbered perhaps 50,000, though some contemporary and modern historians say 100,000; another passage gives perhaps 45,000 fighting troops, including Janissaries, Timarli cavalry and conscripted Balkan levies, and says Suleiman and Ibrahim left Constantinople in April with 100,000 men.

On 26 August, at a conference in Louis's camp at Bata, the chancellor Stephen Brodarics advised waiting for reinforcements from Austria and Bohemia, but impetuous nobles persuaded the king to fight at once. The war council did not wait for the Croatian and Transylvanian forces, a few days' march away, and chose an open but uneven plain with marshes. The Hungarians formed two lines: mercenary infantry and artillery in the centre of the first with heavy cavalry on both flanks, levy infantry and reserve cavalry in the second.
sections.course:
The battle began on the afternoon of 29 August. The Hungarians were well rested, while the Ottomans had just finished a strenuous march in the summer heat. Confident in their heavy cavalry, the Hungarians hoped to break the Ottoman line by a direct assault. Early in the afternoon Archbishop Pál Tomori led a charge that drove back the Ottoman front line and caused disorder among the irregulars.

Ibrahim Pasha, who commanded the Ottoman centre, fell back in a controlled manoeuvre, forming a crescent that exposed the flanks of the advancing Hungarian cavalry; contemporaries credited him with a feigned retreat. As Louis and the reserves moved up in support, the Ottomans counterattacked with cavalry and light infantry from both wings, while Janissaries and artillery opened concentrated fire from prepared positions. According to some accounts, Hungarian bullets struck Suleiman's cuirass during the charge. The Hungarians, advanced too far and too fast, were encircled and under musket and cannon fire, and within two hours their lines collapsed.

King Louis tried to flee but drowned in the marshy ground near the Csele stream, weighed down by his armour; his body was found weeks later, buried in the mud. Suleiman is reported to have expressed regret for the young king's death. Among the dead were thousands of Hungarian soldiers and over 1,000 nobles, including seven bishops and twenty-eight barons.
sections.aftermath:
It is estimated that over 14,000 Hungarian troops died, including 4,000 cavalry and 10,000 infantry, and a further 2,000 prisoners were executed. That evening Suleiman and his staff did not grasp the scale of the victory, believed they had met only part of the Hungarian forces and kept their army under arms all night. Next day he saw he had won a decisive victory. He stayed four more days at Mohács and executed about 2,000 captured Hungarian nobles, whose bodies were found by archaeologists after 2020.

Queen Mary, at Buda, heard of the defeat on the evening of 30 August and fled to Pozsony with her treasures. The army reached Buda on 11 September; the city surrendered without a fight, but was set on fire on 14 and 15 September together with most of Pest, though orders had been given to spare it. Malkoçoğlu Bali Bey's horsemen murdered the mainly male population with great cruelty. Pécs was plundered and burned. On 13 September the Turks broke into a camp of refugees between Maróth and Dömös and massacred about 25,000 people, including old people, women and children.

Suleiman took the treasures of the Matthias era, including most of the Corvinus Library, to Constantinople, where he arrived on 13 November, keeping only Pétervárad, Illok and Szalankamen. The Hungarian nobility elected two kings, John Zápolya and Ferdinand of Austria. In 1541 the Ottomans decided to occupy Buda. Bohemia and Moravia fell to the Habsburgs, who also held the north and west of Hungary; the Ottomans held central Hungary and suzerainty over Transylvania, a principality from 1571.
sections.sources:
The battle is known from a mixed body of writings, and the figures in them do not agree. Stephen Brodarics wrote a report of it in 1527 for the Polish king Sigismund I, Antal Verancsics wrote an account of the events of Louis's reign, and the Ottoman chroniclers Kemalpasazade, Dselalzade, Pecsevi and Szolakzade, together with Suleiman's war diaries, tell the campaign from the Turkish side. Suleiman is only said to have spoken his words of grief over the king's body. Contemporary records of Louis's preference for retreat are sparse.

The numbers are uncertain. The Ottoman army is put at perhaps 50,000, with some historians at 100,000, and its fighting troops at perhaps 45,000. The Hungarian total at Mohács is 25,000 to 30,000, while the units known to historians, whose data do not allow a reconstruction of the rest of the army, cover fewer men. The dead are put at over 14,000, with a further 2,000 executed prisoners. Some details of the fighting, such as the bullets striking Suleiman's cuirass, appear only in some accounts.

Historians differ on why Hungary lost. Fichtner points to a breakdown of communication between Louis and Ferdinand, Alfred Kohler to the king's lack of vigour, and Stephen Fischer-Galati to Louis's failure to grasp the Turkish threat. Louis's refusal of the Ottoman peace offers is unexplained.
sections.legacy:
Mohács was a decisive Ottoman victory, achieved through planning, firepower and encirclement, and the beginning of sustained Ottoman and Habsburg wars. For all intents and purposes it meant the end of the independent Kingdom of Hungary as a unified entity, and the end of the Jagiellonian dynasty in Hungary and Bohemia. Ferdinand's aim was to create a new empire from his kingdoms, officially named the Austrian Empire only in 1804.

The partition was followed by near constant warfare. Territory held by the Kingdom of Hungary shrank by around 60% during the Ottoman wars. Crusader armies besieged Buda several times between 1530 and 1686. Suleiman died of natural causes in Hungary during the siege of Szigetvár in 1566, and the Ottomans failed at Eger in 1552 and took it only in 1596. The Habsburgs needed Hungary's economic power for these wars; Royal Hungary remained as important economically as the Austrian lands and was Ferdinand's largest source of revenue.

In Hungarian memory Mohács is a national trauma and the turning point in the country's history, summed up in the saying Több is veszett Mohácsnál, 'more was lost at Mohács'. Hungary would only regain its former boundaries in the 19th century, with full independence from Habsburg rule coming after the First World War. The battlefield beside the village of Sátorhely became an official national historical memorial site in 1976, on the 450th anniversary, with a memorial by the architect György Vadász; a reception hall and exhibition building by him was completed in 2011.

summary: At Mohács on 29 August 1526 the Ottoman army of Suleiman the Magnificent encircled and broke the Hungarian army of King Louis II, who drowned in flight. The kingdom was later partitioned, and Hungarians remember the battle as a national tragedy.
notes: The article has no sources section; 'sources' is built from its reference list, its quotations of Kemalpasazade, Brodarics and others, and its own hedges. Thin, and the editor should read it first.

Ottoman strength is inconsistent in the article: perhaps 50,000 (some say 100,000) in preparation, perhaps 45,000 fighting troops in the battle section, 100,000 men leaving Constantinople. All three given.
The article's Hungarian unit list (3,000+1,000+4,500+6,700+5,300+1,500) sums to 22,000, short of 25,000-30,000; I did not add it up.
The executed prisoners are 'about 2,000' in the dead paragraph and 'about 2000 captured Hungarian nobles' later; I gave both as the article does.
The article says 'about 25,000' people massacred at the Maróth/Dömös camp, a very large figure; attributed as the article's own.
The Pécs bishop and the Kemalpasazade quotation on Bács left out for length. Szapolyai's movements, Várday's appeal and the Bács siege left out.
The article says Suleiman 'executed' the 2,000 nobles while elsewhere crediting the executions to the aftermath; the sources section ties both to the same figure.
